title: UDP & Choosing TCP vs UDP
summary: UDP's minimal connectionless model, why some applications want unreliability, and the concrete engineering trade-off of choosing it over TCP.

slides.markdown:
TCP's header carries sequence numbers, ACK numbers, window size, flags — dozens of bytes of bookkeeping. UDP's header is just **8 bytes**: source port, destination port, length, checksum. Nothing else.

No handshake before sending, no acknowledgment after, no retransmission, no ordering guarantee. UDP hands a datagram to IP and moves on — the application gets exactly as much (or as little) reliability as it builds itself.

assets.alt: UDP header fields versus TCP header fields

slides.markdown:
"Unreliable" doesn't mean broken — it means **no guarantee**. A UDP datagram might arrive, arrive late, arrive out of order relative to others, arrive duplicated, or simply vanish, and UDP itself will never tell you which happened.

In practice, on a healthy modern network most datagrams do arrive fine — but an application built on UDP must be written as if any given one might not, because nothing underneath will catch it.

Sounds backwards until you think about **stale data**. In a voice call, a resent 200ms-old audio packet is worse than useless — by the time it arrives, the conversation has moved on; better to drop it and play the next one.

Voice, live video, competitive gaming, and DNS all share this trait: a late retransmission is often worse than a gap. TCP's retransmit-and-wait model actively hurts these use cases by blocking newer, more relevant data behind an old lost packet.

Choosing UDP doesn't mean choosing chaos — it means choosing **which** reliability you build, instead of inheriting TCP's one-size-fits-all version.

A video call might add just enough sequencing to detect (not fix) loss and conceal it with buffering; a game might add just acknowledgment for critical state changes but not for every position update. This is exactly what protocols like QUIC do at scale — reimplement only the reliability pieces that matter. See [QUIC & HTTP/3](quic-http3).

| | TCP | UDP |
|---|---|---|
| Connection | Handshake required | None — send immediately |
| Ordering | Guaranteed | Not guaranteed |
| Reliability | Retransmits lost data | None built in |
| Overhead | Higher (20+ byte header, ACKs) | Minimal (8-byte header) |
| Typical use | Web, email, file transfer | DNS, voice, video, gaming |

Decide by asking: does this application need every byte, in order, no matter the delay (TCP) — or does it need the freshest data now, tolerating gaps (UDP)?

UDP's checksum covers the header and data, detecting corruption in transit — but in **IPv4 it's optional** (a sender can set it to zero, meaning "not computed"), while in **IPv6 it's mandatory**, because IPv6 dropped IP-level header checksums entirely and leans on the transport layer instead.

Either way, the checksum only *detects* corruption — a failed check means the datagram is silently discarded, not corrected or retransmitted by UDP itself.

TCP is inherently one-to-one — a connection has exactly one sender and one receiver. **Multicast** (one-to-many, opt-in group) and **broadcast** (one-to-all on a subnet) only make sense over a connectionless model like UDP, since there's no single peer to hold a TCP state machine with.

Real examples: IPTV-style video distribution using multicast, and DHCP's initial broadcast discovery before a client even has an IP address.

slides.sectionTitle: A lost packet: silent vs retransmitted
slides.markdown:
Same network, same lost packet, opposite outcomes. Over **UDP**, the datagram is simply gone — the application either notices the gap itself or never knows. Over **TCP**, the missing segment is detected (timeout or duplicate ACKs) and automatically resent.

This single picture is the crux of the TCP-vs-UDP decision: do you want the network layer to silently drop and move on, or to notice and recover — at the cost of time?

assets.alt: A lost UDP packet vanishing versus a lost TCP segment being retransmitted

slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "UDP is faster, so I'll use it for my app and get better performance for free."

**Why it's wrong:** UDP is faster *per packet* since it skips handshakes and acknowledgments — but if your app actually needs ordering or lossless delivery, you'll end up reimplementing a worse version of what TCP already does well.

**Correct model:** pick UDP only when you've designed for loss, reordering, and duplication — not as a default speed hack. Need TCP's guarantees? Use TCP, or QUIC for UDP's flexibility with built-in reliability.
